text: Matvey Isaakovich Blanter (10 February [O.S. 28 January] 1903 – 27 September 1990) was a Soviet composer and one of the most prominent creators of popular songs and film music in the Soviet Union. He composed over two thousand songs and remained active as a composer until 1975. Born in Pochep, then in the Chernigov Governorate of the Russian Empire, to a Jewish craftsman, Blanter studied piano and violin at the Kursk Higher Music School and continued his education in Moscow from 1917 to 1919, studying violin and composition. His early works in the 1920s included light dance and jazz music, such as "John Gray" (1923), a foxtrot that became a major hit. In the 1930s, under increasing ideological pressure, Blanter shifted to composing Soviet propaganda songs and became a key figure in the development of the Soviet "mass song." Among his notable works from this period are "The Song of Shchors" (1935), which tells the story of Ukrainian Red Army commander Nikolai Shchors, and "Partisan Zheleznyak" (1936), which blends military marching rhythms with a mournful ballad describing Commander Zheleznyak's heroic death, opening and closing with a stanza about his lonely burial mound in the steppes. Other significant songs include "Youth" (1937), a cheerful marching song asserting that "right now, everyone is young in our young, beautiful country"; "Stalin Is Our Battle-Glory" (1937), a widely performed hymn to Joseph Stalin; and "The Football March" (1938), whose music is still performed at the start of every football match in Russia. In 1938, Blanter began a long collaboration with poet Mikhail Isakovsky, producing the world-renowned "Katyusha," which combines elements of a heroic battle song and a peasant lament. In the song, a young woman named Katyusha sings of her beloved, compared to "a gray eagle of the steppes," who is far away serving on the Soviet border; the theme emphasizes that the soldier will protect the Motherland while the girl preserves their love. Though joyful and full of imagery of a fertile, blooming land, the song also conveys the sense that the motherland is under threat, and it gained fame during World War II as an inspiration to defend one's land. In 1937, Pravda called for thousands of Soviet girls to work in the Far East to help build military defenses, and Blanter was commissioned to write the operetta *On the Bank of the Amur River* to celebrate the initiative; it premiered at the Moscow Operetta Theatre in 1939 and was broadcast by Moscow Radio and performed nationwide. In early 1945, Blanter accompanied the Red Army to Berlin and was commissioned by Stalin to compose a symphony about the capture of Berlin. However, when Vasily Chuikov met with a German delegation led by Hans Krebs to negotiate surrender, Chuikov had war correspondents pretend to be members of his staff to appear more intimidating. Blanter, wearing civilian clothes, could not pass as an officer and was shoved into a closet just before the delegation arrived. He remained there for most of the meeting and eventually collapsed from lack of air, falling out of the closet into the room just as the delegates were leaving, embarrassing Chuikov and shocking the Germans. Blanter also composed several popular wartime songs, including "The Enemy Burned Down His Home" (1945), which depicts a soldier returning to find his entire family dead; the song was deemed too pessimistic by authorities and banned until it was performed for the first time in 1961. Postwar works include "The Migratory Birds Are Flying" (1949), a patriotic song in which the narrator watches migratory birds fly away and declares that he can think of no better place than the Motherland, and "Dark-Eyed Cossack Girl" (Russian: Черноглазая казачка), written specifically for bass-baritone Leonid Kharitonov. In 1983, Blanter joined the Anti-Zionist Committee of the Soviet Public, an organization established as an anti-Zionist propaganda tool. He died in Moscow in 1990 and was buried at Novodevichy Cemetery. Ayn Rand's 1936 novel *We the Living*, set in Petrograd between 1923 and 1925, includes a passage highlighting the immense popularity of "John Gray." In the 1966 novel *The Last Battle*, Cornelius Ryan notes that Blanter accompanied the Red Army into Berlin during the final days of the war and the collapse of Nazi power. In the 2004 film *Downfall*, Blanter has a minor role and is portrayed by Boris Schwarzmann, depicted as being stuffed into the closet of Vasily Chuikov's office, who is in a rush to meet Nazi general Hans Krebs.
